I would treat this as a cash-forward continuity upsell, not as a simple discount. The idea can work: buy-X-get-Y-free is specifically useful when customers can sensibly buy more duration or quantity, and it can pull cash forward, but the source warns to manage the prepaid cash, deliver on the promise, and cap this kind of recurring prepay offer rather than converting too much of the base at once [buy-x-get-y:5] [buy-x-get-y:4].

For your current numbers, six refill months at $55 is $330 collected up front. With about $28 gross profit per refill month, your implied product/fulfillment cost is about $27 per month. That means:

- Six paid months, no bonus: $168 gross profit before CAC.
- Six paid plus one bonus month: $141 gross profit before CAC.
- Six paid plus two bonus months: $114 gross profit before CAC.

Your CAC is $48, so even the two-bonus-month version appears to recover CAC on gross profit. The real risk is cash timing: if inventory/fulfillment cost for 7-8 months lands early, you may collect $330 but immediately owe roughly $189-$216 in delivery cost before you have earned the months operationally.

Before doing it, I would check five things:

1. Escrow the obligation mentally, even if not literally. Do not spend all the prepay cash as profit. Reserve the cost of every promised shipment plus a cushion for spoilage, refunds, failed fulfillment, and support.

2. Cap the rollout. The framework suggests this is a good fast-cash play when the business is healthy, but warns against using it as survival cash and suggests capping recurring-customer prepay exposure around 10% [buy-x-get-y:4] [buy-x-get-y:5]. I would start with existing subscribers or high-repeat buyers first, not cold traffic.

3. Make the bonus months earn their cash-flow role. Bulk continuity prepay can materially boost 30-day profit, but the offer should be sized around how much cash you need to offset CAC and fund acquisition [continuity-bonus:9]. For you, the question is not "will it sell?" but "does it improve first-30-day cash after early inventory purchases?"

4. Separate contribution profit from bank balance. On paper, buy six get two still has positive gross profit. In the bank, it may be dangerous if you must buy the inventory immediately, your 3PL bills early, or a large share of customers take the deal at once.

5. Protect retention behavior. Prepay buyers are often good buyers later, and the source notes they can still be offered other relevant products after prepaying [buy-x-get-y:4]. Do not make the refill bundle so broad that it removes the natural next purchase, such as a premium routine, seasonal add-on, or sensitive-skin accessory.

My recommendation: test a capped version first, probably "buy 6, get 1" before "buy 6, get 2," and only sell as many as your cash reserve can fulfill if every shipment cost came due early. To size the cap precisely, I need three numbers: how many bonus months you are considering, whether inventory for all promised months must be purchased up front, and your available cash reserve after normal operating expenses.
